overview.text: Deuterium (hydrogen-2, written ²H or D) is a stable, naturally occurring but minor isotope of hydrogen. Its nucleus has one proton and one neutron; the most common hydrogen isotope, protium, has only a proton, so deuterium is roughly twice as massive. Its atomic mass is about 2.014, and its proportion varies among natural hydrogen sources. Deuterium is important in research: fusion scientists investigate combining it with radioactive tritium, a reaction that produces helium and an energetic neutron, as a possible route to future power. The isotope’s experimental identification in 1931 provided striking evidence that hydrogen, too, has isotopes.

key_facts.text: Deuterium is the minor stable isotope ²H; its symbol is D, and its listed atomic mass is about 2.014 Da.
A deuterium nucleus contains one proton and one neutron. The most common hydrogen isotope, protium, has one proton and no neutrons.
Deuterium’s natural abundance varies among hydrogen sources; CIAAW lists a range rather than one universal percentage.
Experiments reported in 1932 established hydrogen-2’s existence; Harold Urey, George Murphy, and Ferdinand Brickwedde identified its spectral lines in enriched samples.
Deuterium-tritium fusion is being investigated as a possible future energy source; the reaction produces helium and an energetic neutron.
